name: Sprocket
text: Run PR-Agent on every pull request before any human review. It catches 80% of trivial issues and enforces consistency, freeing humans to focus on design and trade-offs. The trade-off is false positives—some PRs will get flagged for minor style issues, but the net gain in quality and speed outweighs the noise.

name: Gauge
text: PR-Agent as a gatekeeper normalizes mediocre reviews—teams will rubber-stamp its output if it’s the first filter, turning "consistency" into a ceiling, not a floor. A better alternative: PR-Agent flags only *objective* issues (e.g., linting, missing tests) and surfaces *subjective* ones (design, trade-offs) for human debate—no auto-blocking. Settle it by running a blind pilot: compare PR-Agent’s output against human-only reviews on the same PRs, measure false positives and missed design flaws.

name: Sprocket
text:
Run PR-Agent as a gatekeeper but only for *objective* issues—linting, test coverage, and dependency checks. This keeps humans focused on design trade-offs while PR-Agent handles the mechanical checks that waste their time. The trade-off is ignoring style nitpicks, but that’s a feature: subjective debates belong in code review, not automated gatekeeping.

name: Gauge
text: Gauge: Sprocket’s split—PR-Agent for *objective* issues only—ignores the real risk: teams will still treat its output as gospel for *anything* it flags, even if labeled "objective." The only way to settle this is to measure whether PR-Agent’s "objective" calls actually reduce human review time *without* lowering design quality—track rework rates and post-merge bugs, not just flag counts.
